title: Inaugural Gary V. Désir Lecture Highlights Translational Science | Newswise - Newswise
content: Browse experts available to comment on breaking news Request an expert contact, get responses directly to your inbox Find an expert by topic in a comprehensive database Newswise — The Department of Internal Medicine at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) honored former department chair Gary V. Désir, MD, with the inaugural Gary V. Désir Lecture, on September 24, 2026, featuring physician-scientist Richard Kibbey, MD, PhD. The lectureship was established by Vincent Quagliarello, MD, vice chair for education and academic affairs in the Department of Internal Medicine, in recognition of Désir’s leadership and his dedication to translating basic science into practical therapies for patients. Désir, the Paul B. Beeson Professor of Medicine, served as chair of the Department of Internal Medicine from 2013 to 2025. He is currently vice provost for faculty development at Yale University, a position he has held since 2020. He joined the YSM faculty in 1986 after earning his MD at YSM and completing his residency and fellowship at Yale New Haven Hospital. In his opening remarks, Wolfram Goessling, MD, PhD, current chair of the Department of Internal Medicine, reflected on Désir’s contributions to the department and university. “His impact both on our institution, university-wide, and on our department has really been amazing,” Goessling said, noting Désir’s leadership during the COVID-19 pandemic. Goessling also highlighted the theme of the lectureship: translating findings from the lab to the clinic. “Gary’s discovery of renalase and its applications in various medical conditions is a hallmark and emblematic of that effort that we have here at Yale,” he said. Gerald I. Shulman, MD, PhD, the George R. Cowgill Professor of Medicine (Endocrinology) and professor of cellular and molecular physiology, then introduced Kibbey, describing the lecture as a deserving tribute to Désir’s career as a physician-scientist. “This lectureship honors Gary Désir for his extraordinary contributions to Yale as an accomplished physician-scientist, a visionary academic leader, and a steadfast advocate for the people and mission of our medical community,” he said. “It is especially fitting that this inaugural lecture is being delivered by someone who so clearly embodies the physician-scientist tradition that Gary has championed throughout his career.” Shulman added that both Désir and Kibbey are inspired by the patient to understand pathogenesis and develop solutions. In his presentation, “Mitochondrial Satiety: Implications for the Treatment of Obesity,” Kibbey discussed small molecules that may help regulate long-term body-weight homeostasis by reaching the midbrain. He described the potential for a once-daily small molecule pyruvate kinase activator that integrates metabolic signals with nutrient-stimulated hormone signals to improve the treatment of obesity and diabetes without muscle loss. One of the key features of this therapeutic strategy is that it is anabolic for muscle, in contrast to other obesity treatments that lead to muscle loss. Kibbey is the Ensign Professor of Medicine (Endocrinology and Metabolism) and professor of molecular and cellular physiology. He also serves as co-vice chief for research in the Section of Endocrinology and Metabolism, associate director of the Yale Program in Translational Biomedicine, and director of the Yale Program for Mitochondrial Biology and Intermediary Metabolism. The Department of Internal Medicine at Yale School of Medicine is among the nation's premier departments, bringing together an elite cadre of clinicians, investigators, educators, and staff in one of the world's top medical schools. To learn more, visit Internal Medicine. title: Jake Bauers v. Yoshinobu Yamamoto: A Breakdown - Brew Crew Ball
content: Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto is one of the best pitchers, and one of the best postseason performers, in baseball. In Game 2 of last year’s NLCS, Yamamoto mystified the Brewers offense, throwing 111 pitches en route to a complete-game victory. Less than two months ago, he went six innings and struck out nine in a game the Dodgers went on to win. Add Brew Crew Ball as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. Yesterday, in Game 2 of the 2026 NLCS, he couldn’t make it through the third inning. It took Yamamoto 45 pitches to get through the order once. The second time around, he struck out leadoff man Jackson Chourio on three pitches, but the Brewers kept grinding. Brice Turang worked a six-pitch walk, then William Contreras flew out after battling for seven pitches. With Yamamoto at 61 pitches through 2 2/3 innings, Jake Bauers came to the plate and put together the best at-bat of the series, culminating in a 12-pitch walk. One batter later, Christian Yelich laced a single up the middle that forced Dodgers manager Dave Roberts to go to his bullpen in the third inning. Bauers’ at-bat was a perfect microcosm of the Brewers’ strategy against Yamamoto. Nobody in baseball is going to out-pitch Yamamoto over nine playoff innings, so the Brewers set out to make sure he never got the chance. Unlike last year’s NLCS, when they were uncharacteristically happy to chase (and miss) pitches out of the zone, this time they tried to make him beat them in the strike zone. Of Yamamoto’s 75 pitches, 35 were in the strike zone and 40 were out of it. The Brewers swung and missed just four times, compared to 12 called strikes. They weren’t swinging through anything; they took pitches early and made contact late to try and drive up Yamamoto’s pitch count. The box score credits Yamamoto with 46 strikes and 29 balls. Take away the 16 called and swinging strikes, and that leaves 30 strikes that were either fouled off or put in play. Yamamoto faced 14 batters, striking out one and walking two, so 11 balls were put in play. That means 19 of his pitches ended in foul balls, almost exactly a quarter of his total pitches. Nine of those foul balls, across two at-bats, were courtesy of Bauers. Somehow, the box score doesn’t quite capture how impressive Bauers’ second at-bat was. Yamamoto, who throws six different pitches, is one of the filthiest pitchers in baseball. Making it through 12 pitches against him is, quite literally, something nobody in Major League Baseball had ever done. This might look like an easier take on TV, but one reason Yamamoto is so effective is how his splitter and four-seamer play off each other. A fastball in that location would stay in the zone for a strike. The splitter looks like it might catch the bottom of the zone, then dives away from the left-handed Bauers and into the dirt. Bauers recognizes the spin and takes it for ball one. Yamamoto comes back with a perfectly located splitter that catches the outside corner. His fastball usually sits about five mph faster than his splitter, so if Bauers had mistaken this for a middle-out fastball, he’d have been out in front and on top of it, likely rolling over into a weak groundout two pitches into the at-bat. Instead, he takes it for strike one. After two straight splitters at 91, a high fastball can look like a mistake worth jumping on. But at five mph harder than the splitter, this one keeps riding up and out of the zone. As mentioned, Yamamoto gets a lot of quick outs by letting his fastball play off his splitter. A more swing-happy hitter probably swings under this one for strike two, or worse, pops it up. Bauers clearly wants to swing, but he lays off for ball two. While Yamamoto’s splitter is his main change-of-speed weapon, he also has a big, loopy curveball in his back pocket. It sits in the mid-70s, so after a 96-mph fastball, it can almost look like it’s in slow motion. Just like the previous fastball, Yamamoto starts it high. A hitter who’s geared up for velocity can easily get out in front of it and roll over, but Bauers doesn’t bite. The problem is that this time, the pitch doesn’t stay up — it drops into the zone, and for the first time in the at-bat, Yamamoto has the upper hand. Strike two. Yamamoto goes back to the splitter, similar to the second pitch. This one starts high, then breaks down and away from Bauers, but it doesn’t end up in the zone. With two strikes, plenty of hitters would protect the plate and chase it. Bauers takes it to run the count full. Yamamoto reaches back for a little extra and tries to blow a high-and-tight fastball by Bauers. Bauers catches up to it just enough to fight it off foul. Yamamoto tries to mess with Bauers’ timing again with a nasty curveball, about 20 mph slower than the fastball, that would have just caught the bottom inside corner. Bauers, out ahead of it, manages to slow himself down just enough to foul it off. Yamamoto throws his first sinker of the at-bat, and it almost gets Bauers, who swings defensively and pops it up into foul territory down the left-field line. Neither Max Muncy nor Teoscar Hernández can quite get to it, so Bauers lives to see another pitch. At this point, Bauers is just playing pepper. In an impressive display of bat control, he gets inside another high-and-tight fastball and fouls it off. Bauers looks to be sitting on this one and gets a good chunk of it, but the roughly four-mph change of speed between this cutter (the first of the plate appearance) and the previous fastball throws off his timing just enough. His line drive goes foul down the first-base line. Based on the way he gears up to swing, Bauers is probably thinking fastball or cutter again. But surprise, it’s a splitter! At the last second, it dives down and away, and Bauers — in full “protect the plate” mode — manages to foul it into the dirt with the very end of his bat. Bauers has swung at the last six pitches, so Yamamoto goes back to his curveball, hoping Bauers will chase one more time. He starts it at the bottom of the zone and lets it dive below. Bauers recognizes the curveball and lays off for ball four. Bauers faced five different pitches, fouled off at least one of each, and ended the at-bat with a 12-pitch walk, something no hitter had ever done against Yoshinobu Yamamoto. The Brewers didn’t beat one of the best pitchers in baseball by hitting him hard. They beat him by refusing to let him put them away, and no one refused harder than Jake Bauers. title: The 2028 Dodge Charger Will Gain the Hemi Supercharged 6.2-liter V-8, Internal Documents Show - Car and Driver
content:
Hellcat power will reportedly return to the gas-fed Charger, where it’ll send power exclusively to the rear wheels. Prepare for your houses to be filled with the sound of supercharged V-8 engines thundering down your neighborhood streets once again. The 2028 model year is slated to herald the return of the Hemi supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 to the Dodge Charger lineup, internal documents obtained by MoparInsiders show. Welcome back to the roads, Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat; you have been missed. According to the report, the document shows that the Hellcat powertrain will be made available for the four-door Charger sedan as well as the two-door coupe. In either form factor, the powerplant will be mated to the ZF 8HP95 eight-speed automatic transmission. Perhaps most excitingly, though, is that the document also reports that unlike the Hurricane-powered Chargers of today, which come standard with an all-wheel-drive layout, the Hellcat Chargers are being developed as rear-drivers. See all results for new 2028 Dodge Charger for sale and new 2028 Dodge Charger for sale near 85032 The document shows that the 2028 lineup will retain the 3.0-liter Hurricane inline-six in three configurations. The 420-hp Standard Output is back, as are the 550-hp High Output and 600-hp High-Output plus (Super Bee) variants. They’ll be joined by the Charger Daytona’s electric offerings, and rounded out with the return of the supercharged 6.2-liter SRT engine. Sadly, the document leaves the 6.2’s specs a mystery. One possibility is that Dodge brings the Hellcat Hemi back unchanged. That would mean a stout 717 horsepower. Another entirely plausible option is for Dodge to fit the flagship Charger with the updated 777-hp version of the 6.2 found in the 2027 Ram 1500 SRT TRX pickup. Car and Driver reached out to Dodge for confirmation of the internal document and its content, but we haven’t heard back at the time of publishing. We will update this story if we learn more. title: Take a Tour of Azul V, Below Deck's New Yacht for Season 13: “Where the Magic Happens” (VIDEO) - Bravo
content: Chief stew Fraser Olender gives an inside look at Below Deck Season 13's yacht, Azul V, during an exclusive Bravo Insider tour. A new yacht carried the crew and charter guests through the sparkling waters of Thailand on Below Deck Season 13, and chief stew Fraser Olender took us on an exclusive Bravo Insider video tour of M/Y Azul V (watch above). We also got a look at the vessel during Below Deck’s season premiere. Below Deck airs on Mondays at 8 p.m. EST/PST on Bravo. Episodes stream next day on Peacock. “It’s a 48 meter based in Malaysia, and we brought it here to Thailand,” Captain Kerry Titheradge detailed during the Oct. 12 episode. “And the interior layout of this boat is amazing. The deck space is incredible. The sun deck is vast and open.” Not only is the yacht new to Fraser and the crew, it’s also new to Kerry. “I haven’t driven this boat before, so I’ve got to get familiar with that,” he admitted. Fraser didn’t hold back his enthusiasm for Azul V, joking to Kerry, “I feel like I’ve got a new toy. Can I run around the boat?” Close up views of, Azul V., the Below Deck Season 13 yacht. The main salon on Azul V., the Below Deck Season 13 yacht. During Fraser’s exclusive Azul V tour (watch above), he began just like he would with any charter guests: in the sky lounge and main sitting area. Decked out in earthy, calming tones with pops of color in the pillows, the large wraparound couch was complimented by round tables, chairs, a television and even a small bar. RELATED: Captain Kerry Issues New Below Deck Crew a Stern Warning About “Dangers” Looming: “Be Aware…” The sun deck on Azul V., the Below Deck Season 13 yacht. Fraser called the sun deck his “favorite part” of Azul V, and added, “This is where the magic happens.” Fraser then called another guest favorite—the hot tub—the “cold tub,” and explained why: “We don’t turn it on, because in Thailand, it’s extremely warm, and we don’t want to heat ourselves up any more than we already are.” The dining area on Azul V., the Below Deck Season 13 yacht. Fraser made it clear where he stands on indoor versus deck meal service on Azul V: indoor all the way. “This is my preferred location for all meal service, breakfasts, lunches and dinners,” he noted of the dining room during the tour. A big reason why includes the dining room's proximity to the galley, so it’s easier to keep the food hot. “Life is a lot easier when we’re serving here,” he added. RELATED: Captain Kerry Titheradge and Fraser Olender Tease Below Deck Season 13: "Biggest Surprise..." (EXCLUSIVE) General Views of the kitchen galley on Azul V, the Below Deck Season 13 yacht. Although the Azul V galley is chef Moe Vilomar’s domain, Fraser admitted there’s tons of “foot traffic” in this particular galley as he shared behind-the-scenes details. “It links the dining room, the pantry, the other pantry, and the sky lounge,” he explained. “I’m sure that chef is not too happy with us using this as a walkway, but, we have no choice.” When it comes to the crew mess, Fraser noted it’s a “very small space.” He continued, “I don’t think it can actually fit the whole crew in one seating.” Adding to his tour of the crew areas, Fraser showed off the laundry room, which he called “the heartbeat of the vessel.” General Views of the primary suite on the Azul V, the Below Deck Season 13 yacht. The tour of Azul V included the primary suite, which Fraser pointed out is called “the diamond suite.” It includes two walk-in wardrobes for primary guests, as well as “a fabulous, very large bathroom” with a big soaking tub and shower. Fraser highlighted that all the guest accommodations on board Azul V are named after gemstones, with the second-largest suite nicknamed “the sapphire suite.” Fraser admitted the sapphire suite is his personal favorite guest room, as he described it as “adorable.” During the Season 13 premiere, Kerry admitted that he "debated this boat, because it's an older vessel." However, he concluded, "It's absolutely perfect for what we're doing in Thailand." However, Kerry quickly ran into issues on the first charter when one of the engines stalled twice. "It's an older boat. This uses compressed air to start the engine. We only have three starts per tank. If it stalls three times, it's not starting the fourth time. Not good." Fraser also opened up about his private life during Below Deck Season 13’s premiere, and spoke on his split from Matt Rogers for the first time.
